name: Ego depletion
statement: Exerting self-control drains a limited resource, so someone who has just resisted one temptation does worse at the next task that needs willpower.
meaning: The strength model treats self-control as a fuel tank rather than a skill. Resisting a biscuit, suppressing an emotion or forcing attention onto a dull task all draw on the same supply, and the supply runs down within minutes. The prediction that made the model famous is specific and testable: performance on a second, unrelated self-control task should fall simply because a first one was performed. That state of reduced capacity is what ego depletion names.

origin.who: Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Mark Muraven and Dianne M. Tice
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper asked the question in its title: "Ego depletion: Is the active self a limited resource?" The model became one of the most influential ideas in social psychology, and a 2010 meta-analysis of 83 studies by Hagger, Wood, Stiff and Chatzisarantis in Psychological Bulletin reported a medium-sized effect across the literature.

evidence: Almost every test uses the same shape, the sequential-task paradigm: participants perform an initial task demanding self-control, then a second unrelated one, and the second task's performance is compared against a control group who skipped the first. Hundreds of experiments of this form were published, and the 2010 meta-analysis pooled 83 of them into a medium-sized effect. Carter and McCullough reapplied small-study corrections to that same body of data in 2014 and found what they called very strong signals of publication bias, with an indication that the effect was no different from zero. Their analysis is what prompted the field to test the paradigm directly rather than pool it again.

replication.headline: Twenty-three laboratories ran the same preregistered protocol on 2,141 people and found an effect indistinguishable from zero.
replication.detail: The Registered Replication Report used a single standardised protocol, agreed in advance, based on a sequential-task design from Sripada and colleagues. The depleting task was the letter "e" task: the depletion group had to press a button for words containing an "e" but withhold the response when the "e" sat next to or one letter from a vowel, while the control group simply responded to every "e". The second task was the multi-source interference task, and the primary outcome was variability in reaction times on its incongruent trials. Pooled across all 23 labs by random-effects meta-analysis the estimate was d = 0.04, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.07 to 0.15. That interval spans zero and rules out an effect of the size the earlier literature reported. The manipulation itself did something: the depletion version of the letter task cut accuracy heavily (d = -1.82) and was rated as harder and more frustrating than the control version. Roy Baumeister was one of three researchers who vetted the protocol before it ran. It tests one protocol run identically everywhere, not every version of the paradigm ever published.

study.cite: Hagger, M. S., Chatzisarantis, N. L. D., Alberts, H., et al. (2016). A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573.

limits: No original effect size is printed in the fields above, because the 2010 meta-analysis is paywalled and its abstract at PubMed carries no figure. Its pooled estimate of d = 0.62 is quoted here from the replication report, which prints it for comparison. That is a number read at one remove, which is why it stays out of the structured fields. The same report gives Carter and colleagues' 2015 rework of that data as g = 0.24 by trim-and-fill and g = 0.003 by the PET regression, also at one remove. Two later multilab tests split on whether anything survives. Vohs and colleagues ran 36 laboratories and 3,531 people in 2021 and their preregistered analysis returned d = 0.06, nonsignificant, with the data four times more likely under the null. Dang and colleagues ran 12 laboratories and 1,775 people on a Stroop task followed by an antisaccade task and found d = 0.10, small and significant. Neither figure is near 0.62.
misreadings: The result is often reported as proof that self-control is not a limited resource. It is not that. It is strong evidence against one specific prediction, tested through one specific task, at the size the literature claimed. Self-control still varies within a person over a day, and that variation still needs an explanation; what has failed is the fuel-tank account of it. The opposite misreading is also common: that a null result at 23 labs is just one study among hundreds. A preregistered protocol run identically across 23 sites is not one study among hundreds. It is the only kind designed so that its answer could not be chosen after the fact. A third error is to treat the 2016 and 2021 multilab reports as one result. They are separate projects with different lead authors, different tasks and different samples, and they happen to agree.
